reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Chiari malformation describes downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils (and, in some types, the brainstem and fourth ventricle) through the foramen magnum
The type I form often presents in adolescence or adulthood with a suboccipital headache classically worsened by coughing, straining, or Valsalva
Associated features can include neck pain, dizziness, imbalance, and lower cranial nerve or brainstem symptoms such as swallowing difficulty
A frequent and important association is syringomyelia, a fluid-filled cavity in the cord that can cause a dissociated (cape-like) sensory loss and hand wasting
The type II form is closely linked with myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus and typically presents in infancy or early childhood
MRI of the brain and whole spine is the key investigation, quantifying tonsillar descent and detecting an associated syrinx
Asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia is often simply monitored, whereas symptomatic cases or those with a progressive syrinx may need posterior fossa decompression
Surgical decompression aims to restore cerebrospinal fluid flow at the craniocervical junction and can stabilise or improve symptoms and an associated syrinx
reference.pathophysiology: Chiari malformations involve herniation of hindbrain structures below the foramen magnum. In the type I form the cerebellar tonsils descend into the upper cervical canal, often with a small or crowded posterior fossa, obstructing normal cerebrospinal fluid movement across the craniocervical junction. This altered CSF dynamics is thought to drive syrinx formation within the spinal cord. The type II form is a more complex hindbrain anomaly with caudal displacement of the brainstem and fourth ventricle, strongly associated with open neural tube defects and hydrocephalus. Symptoms arise from direct compression of neural structures and from disturbed CSF flow.
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain and whole spine to measure tonsillar descent and identify a syrinx
Cine or CSF flow MRI at the craniocervical junction in selected cases
Assessment for hydrocephalus and, in type II, for an associated neural tube defect
Dynamic craniocervical imaging when bony instability or basilar invagination is suspected
redFlags: Progressive brainstem or lower cranial nerve dysfunction, including swallowing or breathing problems
Rapidly enlarging syrinx with advancing weakness or sensory loss
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or associated obstructive hydrocephalus
Acute deterioration in an infant with type II malformation and myelomeningocele
reference.prognosis: Many patients with mild or incidental type I malformation remain stable; symptomatic patients often improve or stabilise after decompression, though an established syrinx and any fixed neurological deficits may only partially recover. Type II outcomes depend heavily on the severity of associated anomalies.
pitfalls: Attributing coughing-related occipital headache to migraine without considering the malformation
Failing to image the whole spine and missing an associated syringomyelia
Over-treating small, asymptomatic incidental tonsillar ectopia
Overlooking coexisting hydrocephalus or craniocervical instability
management: Conservative observation with serial imaging for asymptomatic or incidental type I malformation
Posterior fossa (suboccipital) decompression, with or without duraplasty, as the definitive surgery for symptomatic type I disease or a progressive syrinx
Symptomatic relief of suboccipital headache and neck pain, with advice to limit Valsalva-provoking activities
Treat associated hydrocephalus with cerebrospinal fluid diversion by shunt or endoscopic third ventriculostomy, particularly in type II
Neonatal closure of myelomeningocele and coordinated neurosurgical care for type II malformation
Monitor neurological status and any syrinx with serial MRI of brain and whole spine
Multidisciplinary neurosurgical and neurological input, with escalation for progressive brainstem or lower cranial nerve dysfunction and swallowing difficulty
